title: Vancomycin-Induced HORV: Hemorrhagic Occlusive Retinal Vasculitis
summary: Hemorrhagic Occlusive Retinal Vasculitis (HORV) is a rare, devastating, immune-mediated hypersensitivity reaction triggered by intraocular vancomycin. Characterized by rapid, bilateral, and often irreversible ischemic retinal necrosis, recognizing this condition early and avoiding further vancomycin administration is critical to preventing profound bilateral blindness.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Hemorrhagic Occlusive Retinal Vasculitis (HORV) is an extremely rare, delayed-onset, immune-mediated hypersensitivity reaction triggered by intraocular vancomycin administration (most commonly during routine, uneventful cataract surgery). It is characterized by severe, rapid, and progressive retinal vascular occlusion (both arterial and venous), extensive intraretinal hemorrhages, and profound, often bilateral, vision loss. A primary challenge in HORV is its delayed presentation, which frequently mimics post-operative endophthalmitis, leading to misdiagnosis and devastating secondary injections of vancomycin.

references.citation: Witkin AJ, et al. Vancomycin-Associated Hemorrhagic Occlusive Retinal Vasculitis: Clinical Characteristics of a New Disease Entity. Ophthalmology. 2017.
ASCRS/ASRS Joint HORV Task Force Report. Hemorrhagic Occlusive Retinal Vasculitis Clinical Alert. 2016.

branches: Type III Hypersensitivity (Arthus-type immune-complex deposition within retinal vascular walls)
Prior Exposure / Sensitization (Often sensitized during first eye surgery, causing rapid/severe bilateral reaction upon second eye exposure)
Endothelial Cell Damage (Direct immune-complex-mediated vasculitis leading to thrombosis and necrosis)
Vascular Occlusion (Widespread arteriolar and venular closure, profound capillary non-perfusion)
Secondary Ischemic Cascade (Rapid production of VEGF driving neovascular glaucoma and anterior segment ischemia)

references.citation: Bhadri R, et al. Pathogenesis of immune-mediated vasculitis in drug toxicities. Surveys of Ophthalmology. 2020.

rows: 1 to 8 days post-exposure (often delayed, asymptomatic initial phase)
Painless, rapid, profound visual decline; central scotomas
May present initially as mild blurriness mimicking uveitis
Mild or completely absent (unlike classic infectious endophthalmitis)
Pain may develop secondary to late neovascular glaucoma
Absent (localized Arthus-like hypersensitivity confined to the eye)
No systemic rash, eosinophilia, or renal dysfunction noted

references.citation: Nichols J, et al. Chronology of vision loss in drug-induced retinal vasculitis. Retinal Cases & Brief Reports. 2019.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Anterior Segment: Mild-to-moderate anterior chamber reaction (cell and flare), but minimal hypopyon (disproportionate to the level of posterior segment disease).
Retinal Hemorrhages: Sectoral or diffuse blot, flame, and punctate hemorrhages mimicking CRVO but following a rapid, necrotic pattern.
Vascular 'Ghosting': Severe, rapid attenuation and whitening of both retinal arterioles and venules, progressing to thread-like, bloodless vessels.
Retinal Edema: Concomitant ischemic whitening, macular edema, and optic disc swelling/hyperemia.
Vitreous Inflammatory Activity: Mild-to-moderate vitritis, notably less severe than the dense membranes seen in typical bacterial endophthalmitis.

references.citation: AAO BCSC Section 12: Retina and Vitreous. American Academy of Ophthalmology. 2023-2024.

sections.title: Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Ultra-Widefield Fluorescein Angiography (UWFA) — Immediately perform to identify areas of peripheral and central capillary non-perfusion and vascular occlusion.
Step 2: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) — Assess for diffuse macular edema, subretinal fluid, and hyperreflectivity of inner retinal layers (indicative of acute ischemia).
Step 3: Anterior Chamber / Vitreous Tap — Mandatory if infectious endophthalmitis is suspected; PCR/cultures must be initiated immediately while avoiding empirical vancomycin.
Step 4: B-scan Ultrasonography — Utilized when dense vitreous hemorrhage or severe media opacity prevents adequate visualization of the posterior pole.

references.citation: Joseph A, et al. Imaging characteristics of hemorrhagic occlusive retinal vasculitis. Am J Ophthalmol. 2018.

sections.title: Management & Treatment Protocol
content: Step 1: IMMEDIATE Cessation of Vancomycin — Ensure NO further vancomycin is administered intraocularly, as this is catastrophic.

Step 2: High-Dose Corticosteroids — Initiate aggressive systemic prednisone (1-1.5 mg/kg/day) along with hourly topical prednisolone acetate 1%. Consider intravitreal dexamethasone (0.4 mg) or triamcinolone (4 mg) if infection is strictly ruled out.
Step 3: Urgent Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) — Early PPV should be strongly considered to clear circulating inflammatory cytokines, immune complexes, and toxic intravitreal drug volume.
Step 4: Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP) — Apply prompt, dense peripheral PRP to all ischemic retina detected on angiogram to mitigate the intense drive for neovascularization.
Step 5: Anti-VEGF Adjuvants — Intravitreal anti-VEGF injections (e.g., Aflibercept 2.0mg or Bevacizumab 1.25mg) to control/prevent neovascular glaucoma and decrease macular edema.

references.citation: ASCRS/ASRS Joint Task Force. HORV: Treatment and Management Guidelines. Journal of Cataract & Refractive Surgery. 2018.

sections.title: Surgical Techniques & Settings
sections.content: When performing Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) for HORV, a 23 or 25-gauge sutureless approach is favored. The primary surgical goal is the rapid clearance of vitreous inflammatory mediators, toxic immune complexes, and residual intraocular vancomycin. Induction of a posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) must be executed with extreme caution due to the highly friable, ischemic, and necrotic nature of the retina, which dramatically elevates the risk of iatrogenic giant retinal tears or breaks. Intraoperative endolaser panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) should be carried out aggressively to cover all areas of capillary non-perfusion identified on pre-operative fluorescein angiography.

references.citation: Retina Society Guidelines on Ischemic Retinal Vasculitis Interventions. 2021.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG): Occurs rapidly in up to 50% of untreated or undertreated cases due to extreme ischemic drive.
Phthisis Bulbi: Chronic ciliary body ischemia and low aqueous production can lead to hypotony and globe atrophy.
Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD): Late-stage proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) driven by intense intraocular inflammation.
Vitreous Hemorrhage: Recurrent bleeding from fragile neovascular vessels of the optic disc (NVD) or retina (NVE).
Poor Visual Recovery: More than two-thirds of affected patients are left with permanent legal blindness (visual acuity of 20/200 or worse).

references.citation: Green M, et al. Long-term anatomical and visual outcomes in HORV. Retinal Physician. 2021.

sections.title: Emergency Red Flags
content: NEVER inject empirical intravitreal Vancomycin if post-operative endophthalmitis presents with sectoral retinal hemorrhages or occluded vessels.
A delayed drop in vision (post-operative days 1-15) after an uneventful cataract surgery must be treated as suspect for HORV until proven otherwise.
Rapid rise in Intraocular Pressure (IOP) coupled with rubeosis iridis within 2 weeks of cataract surgery is a hallmark of severe HORV-induced ischemia.
Bilateral sequential cataract surgery performed with prophylactic intracameral vancomycin puts the patient at extreme risk of simultaneous, devastating bilateral HORV.

references.citation: FDA Drug Safety Communication on Intraocular Vancomycin. Food and Drug Administration. 2017.

content.explanation: H = Hemorrhages (dense, blotty, resembling ischemic CRVO); O = Occlusion (severe arteriolar/venular whitening and non-perfusion); R = Redirection (stop all vancomycin administration immediately); V = Visual devastation (high rate of legal blindness or NLP without rapid steroid/PRP intervention).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Check History of Prior Eye Surgery: Always inquire about prior uneventful cataract surgery with intracameral drugs, as sensitization to vancomycin can lead to immediate, aggressive bilateral HORV on the second eye.

Differentiate from Endophthalmitis: If the eye is quiet (minimal hypopyon) but has extensive retinal hemorrhages and whitish/ghost blood vessels, suspect HORV rather than bacterial endophthalmitis. Do NOT inject more vancomycin.
Alternative Prophylaxis: Transition to alternative intracameral antibiotics (such as Cefuroxime or Moxifloxacin) which are not associated with HORV to minimize patient risk.
Early Diagnostic Fluorescein Angiography: Perform UWFA at the earliest suspicion of vasculitis. Demonstrating early capillary drop-out is key to preventing delayed PRP application.

references.citation: Shorstein NH, et al. Alternatives to intracameral vancomycin for endophthalmitis prophylaxis. Journal of Cataract & Refractive Surgery. 2019.

rows: Identified 36 cases of HORV linked specifically to intracameral or intravitreal vancomycin. Established diagnostic criteria.
First official warning advising surgeons of the catastrophic risks of prophylactic vancomycin use.
Detailed 22 eyes of 11 patients showing a strong correlation with prior exposure. High rates of neovascular glaucoma (55%).
Proved the delayed-onset Type III hypersensitivity pathophysiology, discouraging routine use in bilateral surgeries.
Recommended alternative intracameral antibiotics (e.g., Moxifloxacin or Cefuroxime) to eliminate HORV risk.
Substantial shift in cataract surgery protocols worldwide, leading to a decline in routine prophylactic vancomycin use.

references.citation: American Academy of Ophthalmology Clinical Update on HORV. AAO. 2018.

sections.title: Pediatric & Special Populations
sections.content: Special consideration is required for pediatric patients undergoing congenital cataract surgery, where the immune system is highly reactive. Though HORV is exceptionally rare in children, the systemic and ocular consequences of bilateral visual impairment are lifelong and catastrophic. In patients with preexisting systemic autoimmune diseases (such as systemic lupus erythematosus or rheumatoid arthritis) or those who have had prior drug eruptions, the threshold for triggering a type III hypersensitivity reaction to intraocular vancomycin may be lower. In these populations, the use of intracameral moxifloxacin (or preserving aseptic preparation with povidone-iodine alone) is highly recommended over vancomycin.

references.citation: Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus. AAO BCSC Section 6. 2023-2024.

clinicalImages.description: Evaluation of in vitro toxicity of nanoformulations. Human retinal Müller glia (MIO-M1 cell line) were left uninfected or infected with S. aureus (MOI = 10:1) for 2 hours, followed by treatment with nanoformulations for 6 hours. (A) Live-cell imaging was performed using the IncuCyte system, and representative fluorescence (calcein AM stain, green) images were captured to show cell survival in response to indicated treatments. (B) The effect of various nanoformulations or antibiotic (vancomycin) on S. aureus–induced cell death was assessed by measuring LDH release in the culture supernatant. (C) Alamar blue assay was performed by incubating MIO-M1 cells for 24 or 48 hours with various nanoformulations to further assess cytotoxicity. Data were tested for normality using the Shapiro–Wilk test and analyzed by one-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparisons. ****P < 0.0001, as compared to SA; ####P < 0.0001, ##P < 0.01, #P < 0.05; ns, no significant difference as compared to control; n = 3 each experimental condition. Scale: 500 µm (live-cell imaging).
